summary: Tailapa II seized the Rashtrakuta throne in 973 and revived the Chalukya name, ruling the western Deccan from Manyakheta and, after about 1042, from Kalyani. For a century the empire fought the Cholas over Vengi and the Tungabhadra lands, and under Vikramaditya VI (1076–1126) it stretched from the Narmada to the Kaveri country. The Kalachuris took Kalyani in 1157; Someshvara IV won it back around 1183, but the Seunas drove him into exile in 1189 and the Deccan was divided among the Hoysalas, Seunas and Kakatiyas.
details: Tailapa II had been a Rashtrakuta vassal governing Tardavadi, near Bijapur. When the Paramaras of Malwa sacked the Rashtrakuta capital Manyakheta in 972, he seized his chance: in 973 he overthrew Karka II and made Manyakheta his own capital. He claimed descent from the Chalukyas of Badami, a claim historians doubt. Over the next years he defeated rival claimants, won over most Rashtrakuta vassals, and sent his general Barapa to conquer Lata in southern Gujarat. His rule reached from the Narmada to the Tungabhadra.

The most dangerous rival in the north was Munja, king of the Paramaras of Malwa, who had inherited the power that sacked Manyakheta. The two kings fought repeatedly; according to the 14th-century writer Merutunga, Munja defeated Tailapa six times. In the end Tailapa defeated and captured Munja, and had him executed in the mid-990s. The victory secured the empire's northern frontier. Tailapa died around 997 and was succeeded by his son Satyashraya.

In the south the Chola empire of Rajaraja I was expanding fast, and Chalukya and Chola ambitions clashed over the lands along the Tungabhadra and over the Telugu kingdom of Vengi. In 1007 the Chola crown prince Rajendra invaded the Chalukya kingdom and fought Satyashraya at Donur, near Bijapur. Chola inscriptions boast of great destruction, claims that historians treat with caution. The Cholas took Gangavadi and Nolambavadi, in what is now southern Karnataka, and these lands stayed Chola for a century.

Vengi, the delta country between the Krishna and Godavari rivers, was ruled by the Eastern Chalukyas, cousins of the Western Chalukyas but allied to the Cholas by marriage. When its throne fell vacant around 1020, the Western Chalukya king Jayasimha II (1015–1042) backed one claimant and the Chola emperor Rajendra I another. The quarrel over Vengi became the central cause of half a century of Chalukya–Chola warfare. Around 1024 Jayasimha also subdued the Paramaras and the rebellious Yadava king Bhillama in the north.

Jayasimha's son Someshvara I (1042–1068) was an energetic soldier who as a prince had led raids as far as Bihar and Bengal. Around 1042 he moved the capital from Manyakheta to Kalyani (modern Basavakalyan, in northern Karnataka), which gave the dynasty its other name, the Chalukyas of Kalyani. Kalyani grew into a splendid royal city and centre of Kannada and Sanskrit learning. From here Someshvara renewed the wars with the Cholas on the Tungabhadra and in Vengi.

The Chalukya–Chola wars reached a bloody climax at Koppam, on 'the Great River', probably the Krishna, on 28 May 1052 (some date it 1054). The Chola emperor Rajadhiraja I and his brother Rajendra II met Someshvara I's army. Rajadhiraja, riding an elephant, was mortally wounded by Chalukya archers, but Rajendra rallied the Chola troops, crowned himself on the battlefield and routed the Chalukyas; Someshvara fled. Neither side could win outright, and the long war along the Krishna–Tungabhadra frontier went on.

In 1066 the Chalukya prince Vikramaditya raided deep into Chola country, but the Cholas struck back. In 1068 the Chola emperor Virarajendra defeated Someshvara I near Vijayawada, and the Chalukyas lost their hold on Vengi. Soon afterwards Someshvara, suffering from an incurable illness, drowned himself in the Tungabhadra river in a ritual suicide. His eldest son Someshvara II succeeded him but quarrelled with his ambitious younger brother Vikramaditya, and civil war followed.

Vikramaditya VI, backed by the Chola king Virarajendra and by powerful vassals such as the Hoysalas, Seunas and Kadambas of Hangal, defeated his brother Someshvara II and took him captive. He was crowned on 11 February 1076 and launched a new calendar, the Chalukya-Vikrama era, replacing the Shaka era in his records. His fifty-year reign was the empire's golden age. The Kashmiri poet Bilhana wrote his life, the Vikramankadevacharita, and the jurist Vijnaneshwara wrote the Mitakshara, a lasting work of Hindu law, at his court.

Vikramaditya VI kept up the pressure on the Cholas, now ruled by Kulottunga I. In 1085 he invaded the Tamil country and captured Kanchipuram, the old Pallava capital, and in 1088 he conquered parts of Vengi. In the north he subdued the Shilaharas of the Konkan and the Seunas of Devagiri, raided Lata (Gujarat) and checked the Kalachuris of Ratanpur. At its height the empire ran from the Narmada river in the north to the Tumkur and Cuddapah regions in the south, and east to the Godavari districts.

Vengi had changed hands several times: Vikramaditya held it from 1093 until the Cholas retook it in 1099. Late in the reign of the Chola king Kulottunga I, the Chalukyas struck again, and in 1118 their general Anantapala took Vengi and governed it for the emperor. At the same time the Hoysalas took Gangavadi from the Cholas. Vengi stayed Chalukya until about 1124, but after Vikramaditya's death in 1126 the Chola king Vikrama Chola recovered it by 1133.

Vikramaditya VI's son Someshvara III (1126–1138) was more scholar than soldier. In 1129 he completed the Manasollasa, a Sanskrit encyclopedia covering government, warfare, medicine, architecture, cooking, music, sport and the pleasures of kingship. It is a priceless picture of court life in medieval India. But his reign also saw losses: Vengi slipped back to the Cholas, and the great vassal families, the Hoysalas of the south, the Kakatiyas of Telangana and the Seunas of the north, grew steadily more independent.

By the mid-12th century the empire was falling apart. In 1149 the Kakatiya king Prola defeated and captured Tailapa III, a blow to Chalukya prestige. The Kalachuri Bijjala II, a powerful vassal in the north-west, then turned on his overlords and in 1157 took Kalyani. The Chalukya court withdrew south to Annigeri, and the Kalachuris ruled the capital for about twenty years. The empire was reduced to a shadow, while the Hoysalas, Seunas and Kakatiyas acted as independent kings.

When Kalachuri power weakened, Someshvara IV made a final bid to restore the dynasty. Around 1183 he recaptured Kalyani; his general Narasimha killed the Kalachuri king Sankama, and another general, Barma, defeated the Seunas. The revival was brief. The Hoysala king Veera Ballala II defeated Someshvara and the Seuna Bhillama V in the Krishna valley, and in 1189 the Seunas drove Someshvara into exile at Banavasi. The Chalukya empire was divided among the Seunas, Hoysalas and Kakatiyas.
